Healing the brain with light

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
… how to heal brain injuries with light.

Unique Selling Point:
.....a new way of approaching brain injuries, with remarkable effects.

Summary:
The healing benefits of some light frequencies have been known as sued for decades. But few people realize that laser technology has developed to such an extent that some lasers can actually penetrate the human skull and effect healing of brain damage. A Neurologist in Natal has been using this for some time with amazing results on Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, stroke and traumatic brain injury patients. It is called tLLLT -- transcranial low light laser therapy

Further information:
The healing benefits of some light frequencies have been known as sued for decades. But few people realize that laser technology has developed to such an extent that some lasers can actually penetrate the human skull and effect healing of brain damage. A Neurologist in Natal has been using this for some time with amazing results on Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, stroke and traumatic brain injury patients. It is also known as tLLLT – trans cranial low-level laser therapy.

Low-level laser therapy (LLLT) is a form of medicine that applies low-level (low-power) lasers or light-emitting diodes (LEDs) to the surface of the body. Whereas high-power lasers are used in laser medicine to cut or destroy tissue, it is claimed that application of low-power lasers relieves pain or stimulates and enhances cell function. It improves wound healing, arthritic pain and other chronic pain conditions.

However, more recently, low-level laser therapy has also been studied with regard to traumatic brain injury and degenerative brain diseases. One such study is from Harvard:

TRANSCRANIAL LOW-LEVEL LASER (LIGHT) THERAPY FOR BRAIN INJURY.
In: Photomed Laser Surg. 2016 Dec 1;34(12):587-598.
Thunshelle C (Harvard College , Cambridge, Massachusetts, Wellman Center for Photomedicine , Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts) and
Hamblin MR (Department of Dermatology, Harvard Medical School and Harvard-MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology Boston, Massachusetts).
Abstract
BACKGROUND:
Low-level laser therapy (LLLT) or photobiomodulation (PBM) is a possible treatment for brain injury, including traumatic brain injury (TBI).
METHODS:
We review the fundamental mechanisms at the cellular and molecular level and the effects on the brain are discussed. There are several contributing processes that have been proposed to lead to the beneficial effects of PBM in treating TBI such as stimulation of neurogenesis, a decrease in inflammation, and neuroprotection. Both animal and clinical trials for ischemic stroke are outlined. A number of articles have shown how transcranial LLLT (tLLLT) is effective at increasing memory, learning, and the overall neurological performance in rodent models with TBI.
RESULTS:
Our laboratory has conducted three different studies on the effects of tLLLT on mice with TBI. The first studied pulsed against continuous laser irradiation, finding that 10 Hz pulsed was the best. The second compared four different wavelengths, discovering only 660 and 810 nm to have any effectiveness, whereas 732 and 980 nm did not. The third looked at varying regimens of daily laser treatments (1, 3, and 14 days) and found that 14 laser applications was excessive. We also review several studies of the effects of tLLLT on neuroprogenitor cells, brain-derived neurotrophic factor and synaptogenesis, immediate early response knockout mice, and tLLLT in combination therapy with metabolic inhibitors.
CONCLUSIONS:
Finally, some clinical studies in TBI patients are covered.

FIG. 2.
Functional mechanisms of transcranial LLLT. The gene transcription process described in can lead to decreases in neuronal apoptosis and excitotoxicity, and lessening of inflammation and edema, which will help reduce progressive brain damage. Increases in angiogenesis and expression of neurotrophins leading to activation of neural progenitor cells, and increased synaptogenesis may all contribute to the brain repairing itself from damage sustained in the trauma.
Transcranial Low-Level Laser (Light) Therapy for Brain Injury
Photomed Laser Surg. 2016 Dec 1;34(12):587-598.

There are many such studies that show the efficacy of tLLLT in humans as well. It is virtually unknown in traditional neurological practice, but over the last year or two amazing results have been reported from around the globe. tLLLT has strong evidence for many beneficial effects on TBI and stroke in both animal models and human patients. Both acute stroke and acute TBI have a growing number of studies being published showing that tLLLT is an effective means of treating both. The many benefits of tLLLT are thought to be based on several different biological mechanisms:

• Near-infrared PBM functions by improving mitochondrial energy production by stimulating the enzyme CCO and increasing ATP synthesis.

• Laser therapy can result in neuroprotection and help prevent the spread of brain cell death after injury as shown by the long-term development of smaller lesion areas in mice treated with LLLT, when delivered at 4 h post-TBI.

• Protection against toxins, increased cellular proliferation, and reduction in apoptosis and anti-inflammatory and antiedema effects may also contribute to the mechanisms that underlie the beneficial effects of PBM.

• The most exciting prospect is the possibility that tLLLT may stimulate both neurogenesis (the ability of the brain to repair itself) and synaptogenesis (encourage cells to form new synaptic connections). This could lead to the application of tLLLT as a treatment modality for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.

In South Africa up and coming neurologist Dr. Asheligh Bhanjan of Life Entabeni Hospital, Durban has a laser clinic for brain injured people. He reports astounding success with the therapy where severely brain injured individuals and stroke patients show remarkable recovery from their injuries. He also reports astonishing recoveries of people with Parkinson’s and Alsheimer’s. He also reports disappearance of pain for people living with constant pain.

He is willing to be interviewed as has literally dozens of case studies and their families that are willing to speak.

He has been a specialist for about 10 years, and admits that during his specializations years in Neurology they were not introduced to low-level light therapy for TBI or other conditions.

We will also ask a specialist neurologist at a traditional academic institution what they think of the therapy

INTERVIEWEES

• Dr. Asheligh Bhanjan of Life Entabeni Hospital, 083 564 8054
• Prof C-M Schutte, Head Of Department, UP, Steve Biko Academic Hosptial: Tel: 012 354 1082
• Several case studies to be advised by Dr Bhanjan -- we also have video of some of them

The following case studies have been identified by Dr Bhanjan and we are following up with them:

1. Miss Hesme Cronje- (Concussion -with loss of speech )

Age: 22 years
Contact number: 0861711150
Number 2: 315631812 (Susan)

Darryl Webb
He is 73 and has been suffering from Parkinsons for 12 years. The dyskinesia got progressively worse and he had to give up the joy of his life – woodworking. It became too dangerous for him. His GP referred him to Bhanjan and after a few treatments he started to see a difference. It is now 24 treatments later and he is back in his workshop, and able to do what he previously could not do. He speaks really well.

Hesme Cronje
She is 16 and last year she was wit in the head with a rugby ball and suffered a severe concussion. In quick succession she hit her head twice more in unrelated incidents, and lost her speech completely. Speech disorders are common with closed head injuries. It also affected her memory. Doctors told the parents that it would take months for her to regain speech, and that it would probably be partial. Then they heard about the laser treatments and took het to see Dr Bhanjan. After only 4 treatments she started to regain her speech and now after 19 treatments, at the end of the school year she received the prize for the best student in her grade. Important one because of the huge problem with concussion in certain contact sports worldwide. Both Hesme and her mother will speak to us.

Matthew Fernack
He is now 22 and 8 years ago he suffered a fractured skull and TBI when he was hit in the head with a hockey stick. It severely affected his speech and memory and he also developed epileptic seizures which came fairly regularly. He became slow and fell asleep when sitting still. He also suffered severe headaches on a regular basis. They were in Cape Town at the time, but recently move back to Durban where they started treatment with Dr Bhanjan. Matthew’s condition improved markedly -- the headaches are gone, he has not had a seizure in months, he is more awake, his memory is better and he even works. Bth he and his mother Susan will speak to us.

Danile Baijnat:
Adult, shot in spine 18 years ago. Have had chronic pain for 18 years. Was on main management regime, but never without pain. Earlier this year he was put in contact with Dr Bhanjan, and after just a few treatments his pain was basically gone. The treatments made a huge difference and after 18 years, his quality of life has improved markedly. This is also an important aspect because LLLT is also very effective and chronic pain patients benefit a lot. About 20% of people on earth suffers from chronic pain, and the opioid crisis in the US came about because people with chronic pain were given stronger and stronger pain killers. It seems LLLT in situ and used as neural stimulation seems to be more effective that traditional pain management regimes.

Press Release:


Healing the Brain with Light
The healing benefits of some lasers have long been valued – from high-power laser that cuts human tissue to cold laser that enhances cell metabolism and relieves pain. Now pioneering work by one neurologist from Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, using advanced low-light laser therapy to penetrate the skull, is changing the future for patients with traumatic brain injury and degenerative brain diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.
Producer: Eugene Botha | Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


V/O:
Seventy-three-year-old Darrell Webb of Scottburgh in KZN is passionate about woodworking. He loves creating something exquisite with his hands in his workshop. Sadly, 12 years ago, he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
LINK:
Parkinson’s is a nervous system disorder that affects movement. One of the symptoms of the disease is uncontrollable shaking, also known as dyskinesia.
Webb:
It is a very debilitating disease, and it affects not only me, but my partner in crime as well, my wife.
V/O:
And as the disease progresses, the symptoms increase in severity. Ordinarily this would have precluded Webb from pursuing his hobby. And yet, today, he still lives out his passion, even using power tools with precision. Even the assembly of the cut pieces, that require fine motor skills, presents no problem to him.

He says he would not have been able to do any of this were not for this light array. He claims that the light produced by the array, has an effect on his brain and ameliorates his Parkinson’s symptoms – enabling him to practice his beloved hobby.

Dr Ashleigh Bhanjan, a neurologist from Durban introduced Webb to this new and unconventional laser treatment.
Bhanjan:
The response he has had to the therapy is phenomenal. Now he is able to go back to his handcraft work.
V/O:
Webb is even able to run, something which was inconceivable a few months ago.
Bhanjan:
He now has his life back
Webb:
It is new and I believe that it has worked for me. It is worth trying.
LINK:
The use of lasers to treat medical conditions is part of a larger branch in medicine called photomedicine.
V/O:
Photomedicine is the study of the use of light to diagnose and treat disease. This includes laser therapy. The intensity of laser beams can be controlled – from cutting metal to low-level lasers that are safe to use on human skin. In the past, researchers have found that certain frequencies of light have healing properties.
Bhanjan:
This is low intensity light therapy and the review articles describe a term called photobiomodulation treatment. But it is simple: photo = light, bio = life, modulation = change. Changing life using light treatment. It is non-invasive. There is no injury to the tissues because it is non-thermal.
V/O:
Research indicates that red and near infra-red light is able to penetrate tissue. Light consist of photons that are like packages or bundles of energy, and when they penetrate tissue, they interact with the mitochondria found in every human cell.
LINK:
This in turns stimulates photochemical processes in the cells enhancing cell metabolism, reducing inflammation and accelerating the healing of damaged tissue.
Bhanjan:
It has been used for many musculoskeletal conditions including arthritis, sports injuries, chronic neck pain , etcetera. Research in the last few decades has shown that photobiomodulation and low-intensity light therapy to be very effective in peripheral nerve injury as well. They call this photo-neural-modulation where the neurons are now stimulated.
V/O:
This inspired researchers to take a look at the effects of lasers on brain tissue. Harvard University’s Wellman Centre for Photomedicine is one of the leading institutions involved in this research.

The reported effects of laser treatment on all kinds of brain injuries continue to surprise

Sixteen-year-old Hesme Cronje and her mother were shocked by the effects of a random schoolyard incident last year. Hesme was struck in the head by a rugby ball. She was knocked unconscious and sustained a severe concussion. Her mother was called and took her to the hospital.
Hesme:
My head was really sore. I remember coming in and out of consciousness.
V/O:
Several scans were done and she had no structural damage, just a concussion. A few days later she was back in school.
Hesme:
I was still feeling really horrible. I had a horrible headache and I was throwing up every day.
V/O:
During a break she passed out in the bathrooms and fell heavily on her head. When she came to, she could not speak, and was rushed to hospital. More scans were done.
Hesme:
My brain was fully intact, it was just my speech and my headaches and my nausea that was the problem.
V/O:
At the hospital they were introduced to Dr Bhanjan who also assessed her thoroughly. He suggested the new laser therapy. This is Hesme before the first treatment…….. Two hours after her first treatment they again assessed her…….
Hesme:
I went from not being able to say my name to being able to have a conversation. Although my speech was still quite wonky in the sense that it was slurred, but I could speak. I didn’t feel nauseous anymore, I did not have headache, I did not feel as weak, I felt like I was OK. I had another one the following day and the Saturday evening I could have my 16th birthday party.
Claire:
So, it is very interesting to know that light can actually penetrate right through your skull. Is that for real?

Bhanjan:
That is correct, now that was the concern earlier on with this from of therapy, whether it was actually able to penetrate through the skull. And the studies have shown that near-infra red light at a wavelength of about 850 nanometres, is able to penetrate the skull to up to about 5 centimetres. That is plenty of penetration to get into the brain to elicit a chemical cellular response.
V/O:
At 14, Matthew Ferenchack was a talented sportsman when he suffered a broken skull and sustained a traumatic brain injury in a hockey match. This led to refractory epilepsy, frequent hospitalization, speech impairment and severe headaches.
Claire:
Sounds like a mother’s worst nightmare.
Susan:
Yes, that is exactly what it was. The last seven eight years of his life have been really hard and challenging and it has been very difficult to deal with.
V/O:
Dr Bhanjan, who was Ferenchack’s neurologist suggested laser therapy. Initially his mother was very sceptical, but as they had exhausted all conventional options, they decided to try it. Both she and Matthew say the laser treatment worked wonders.
Susan:
It was within 4 treatments that I could see how it was helping him, how it was making his life more positive.
Bhanjan:
Since his therapy he has been headache free, seizure free, he is able to ride his bicycle again, which is another thing. His motor co-ordination improved. So, once again, he is only about 22 and we have given him his life back.
V/O:
However, Prof Lewellen Padayachy, Head of Neurosurgery at the University of Pretoria cautions that cold laser treatment of neurological conditions is new and not used in mainstream medicine.
Padayachy:
It is not something that I am particularly aware of, but I have had a look at the evidence and some of it does appear promising, but it appears to be in a fairly early stage. I looked at a paper from 2019, from one of guys that seem to publish a bit on it. His feeling was, what they say in their conclusion was the pre-clinical studies appear promising, but they suggest further larger clinical studies which is a fair suggestion in medicine, I think.
LINK:
Because it is new, and not part of conventional medicine, medial schemes currently do not pay for treatments.
V/O:
The cost of a treatment is comparable to that of a doctor’s visit or a physiotherapy treatment, and patients usually need a short series of treatments.

But, while research into photobiomodulation continues, Darrell Webb is grateful that he followed Dr Bhanjan’s advice and tried neuro laser treatment.
Webb:
There is improvement. I can hp and skip and jump. Ja, it is really great.
Bhanjan:
To my eyes it is a no-brainer. Coming from a neurologist, it is a no-brainer, because if a treatment is safe, effective, without side effects, why wouldn’t you try it?

Porte TRL43 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 12 January 2020 - Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 03 February 2020 Press Release: Healing the Brain with Light The healing benefits of some lasers have long been valued – from high-power laser that cuts human tissue to cold laser that enhances cell metabolism and relieves pain. Now pioneering work by one neurologist from Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, using advanced low-light laser therapy to penetrate the skull, is changing the future for patients with traumatic brain injury and degenerative brain diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Producer: Eugene Botha | Presenter: Claire Mawisa Script: V/O: Seventy-three-year-old Darrell Webb of Scottburgh in KZN is passionate about woodworking. He loves creating something exquisite with his hands in his workshop. Sadly, 12 years ago, he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. LINK: Parkinson’s is a nervous system disorder that affects movement. One of the symptoms of the disease is uncontrollable shaking, also known as dyskinesia. Webb: It is a very debilitating disease, and it affects not only me, but my partner in crime as well, my wife. V/O: And as the disease progresses, the symptoms increase in severity. Ordinarily this would have precluded Webb from pursuing his hobby. And yet, today, he still lives out his passion, even using power tools with precision. Even the assembly of the cut pieces, that require fine motor skills, presents no problem to him. He says he would not have been able to do any of this were not for this light array. He claims that the light produced by the array, has an effect on his brain and ameliorates his Parkinson’s symptoms – enabling him to practice his beloved hobby. Dr Ashleigh Bhanjan, a neurologist from Durban introduced Webb to this new and unconventional laser treatment. Bhanjan: The response he has had to the therapy is phenomenal. Now he is able to go back to his handcraft work. V/O: Webb is even able to run, something which was inconceivable a few months ago. Bhanjan: He now has his life back Webb: It is new and I believe that it has worked for me. It is worth trying. LINK: The use of lasers to treat medical conditions is part of a larger branch in medicine called photomedicine. V/O: Photomedicine is the study of the use of light to diagnose and treat disease. This includes laser therapy. The intensity of laser beams can be controlled – from cutting metal to low-level lasers that are safe to use on human skin. In the past, researchers have found that certain frequencies of light have healing properties. Bhanjan: This is low intensity light therapy and the review articles describe a term called photobiomodulation treatment. But it is simple: photo = light, bio = life, modulation = change. Changing life using light treatment. It is non-invasive. There is no injury to the tissues because it is non-thermal. V/O: Research indicates that red and near infra-red light is able to penetrate tissue. Light consist of photons that are like packages or bundles of energy, and when they penetrate tissue, they interact with the mitochondria found in every human cell. LINK: This in turns stimulates photochemical processes in the cells enhancing cell metabolism, reducing inflammation and accelerating the healing of damaged tissue. Bhanjan: It has been used for many musculoskeletal conditions including arthritis, sports injuries, chronic neck pain , etcetera. Research in the last few decades has shown that photobiomodulation and low-intensity light therapy to be very effective in peripheral nerve injury as well. They call this photo-neural-modulation where the neurons are now stimulated. V/O: This inspired researchers to take a look at the effects of lasers on brain tissue. Harvard University’s Wellman Centre for Photomedicine is one of the leading institutions involved in this research. The reported effects of laser treatment on all kinds of brain injuries continue to surprise Sixteen-year-old Hesme Cronje and her mother were shocked by the effects of a random schoolyard incident last year. Hesme was struck in the head by a rugby ball. She was knocked unconscious and sustained a severe concussion. Her mother was called and took her to the hospital. Hesme: My head was really sore. I remember coming in and out of consciousness. V/O: Several scans were done and she had no structural damage, just a concussion. A few days later she was back in school. Hesme: I was still feeling really horrible. I had a horrible headache and I was throwing up every day. V/O: During a break she passed out in the bathrooms and fell heavily on her head. When she came to, she could not speak, and was rushed to hospital. More scans were done. Hesme: My brain was fully intact, it was just my speech and my headaches and my nausea that was the problem. V/O: At the hospital they were introduced to Dr Bhanjan who also assessed her thoroughly. He suggested the new laser therapy. This is Hesme before the first treatment…….. Two hours after her first treatment they again assessed her……. Hesme: I went from not being able to say my name to being able to have a conversation. Although my speech was still quite wonky in the sense that it was slurred, but I could speak. I didn’t feel nauseous anymore, I did not have headache, I did not feel as weak, I felt like I was OK. I had another one the following day and the Saturday evening I could have my 16th birthday party. Claire: So, it is very interesting to know that light can actually penetrate right through your skull. Is that for real? Bhanjan: That is correct, now that was the concern earlier on with this from of therapy, whether it was actually able to penetrate through the skull. And the studies have shown that near-infra red light at a wavelength of about 850 nanometres, is able to penetrate the skull to up to about 5 centimetres. That is plenty of penetration to get into the brain to elicit a chemical cellular response. V/O: At 14, Matthew Ferenchack was a talented sportsman when he suffered a broken skull and sustained a traumatic brain injury in a hockey match. This led to refractory epilepsy, frequent hospitalization, speech impairment and severe headaches. Claire: Sounds like a mother’s worst nightmare. Susan: Yes, that is exactly what it was. The last seven eight years of his life have been really hard and challenging and it has been very difficult to deal with. V/O: Dr Bhanjan, who was Ferenchack’s neurologist suggested laser therapy. Initially his mother was very sceptical, but as they had exhausted all conventional options, they decided to try it. Both she and Matthew say the laser treatment worked wonders. Susan: It was within 4 treatments that I could see how it was helping him, how it was making his life more positive. Bhanjan: Since his therapy he has been headache free, seizure free, he is able to ride his bicycle again, which is another thing. His motor co-ordination improved. So, once again, he is only about 22 and we have given him his life back. V/O: However, Prof Lewellen Padayachy, Head of Neurosurgery at the University of Pretoria cautions that cold laser treatment of neurological conditions is new and not used in mainstream medicine. Padayachy: It is not something that I am particularly aware of, but I have had a look at the evidence and some of it does appear promising, but it appears to be in a fairly early stage. I looked at a paper from 2019, from one of guys that seem to publish a bit on it. His feeling was, what they say in their conclusion was the pre-clinical studies appear promising, but they suggest further larger clinical studies which is a fair suggestion in medicine, I think. LINK: Because it is new, and not part of conventional medicine, medial schemes currently do not pay for treatments. V/O: The cost of a treatment is comparable to that of a doctor’s visit or a physiotherapy treatment, and patients usually need a short series of treatments. But, while research into photobiomodulation continues, Darrell Webb is grateful that he followed Dr Bhanjan’s advice and tried neuro laser treatment. Webb: There is improvement. I can hp and skip and jump. Ja, it is really great. Bhanjan: To my eyes it is a no-brainer. Coming from a neurologist, it is a no-brainer, because if a treatment is safe, effective, without side effects, why wouldn’t you try it?

metadata.Further information: The healing benefits of some light frequencies have been known as sued for decades. But few people realize that laser technology has developed to such an extent that some lasers can actually penetrate the human skull and effect healing of brain damage. A Neurologist in Natal has been using this for some time with amazing results on Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, stroke and traumatic brain injury patients. It is also known as tLLLT – trans cranial low-level laser therapy. Low-level laser therapy (LLLT) is a form of medicine that applies low-level (low-power) lasers or light-emitting diodes (LEDs) to the surface of the body. Whereas high-power lasers are used in laser medicine to cut or destroy tissue, it is claimed that application of low-power lasers relieves pain or stimulates and enhances cell function. It improves wound healing, arthritic pain and other chronic pain conditions. However, more recently, low-level laser therapy has also been studied with regard to traumatic brain injury and degenerative brain diseases. One such study is from Harvard: TRANSCRANIAL LOW-LEVEL LASER (LIGHT) THERAPY FOR BRAIN INJURY. In: Photomed Laser Surg. 2016 Dec 1;34(12):587-598. Thunshelle C (Harvard College , Cambridge, Massachusetts, Wellman Center for Photomedicine , Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts) and Hamblin MR (Department of Dermatology, Harvard Medical School and Harvard-MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology Boston, Massachusetts). Abstract BACKGROUND: Low-level laser therapy (LLLT) or photobiomodulation (PBM) is a possible treatment for brain injury, including traumatic brain injury (TBI). METHODS: We review the fundamental mechanisms at the cellular and molecular level and the effects on the brain are discussed. There are several contributing processes that have been proposed to lead to the beneficial effects of PBM in treating TBI such as stimulation of neurogenesis, a decrease in inflammation, and neuroprotection. Both animal and clinical trials for ischemic stroke are outlined. A number of articles have shown how transcranial LLLT (tLLLT) is effective at increasing memory, learning, and the overall neurological performance in rodent models with TBI. RESULTS: Our laboratory has conducted three different studies on the effects of tLLLT on mice with TBI. The first studied pulsed against continuous laser irradiation, finding that 10 Hz pulsed was the best. The second compared four different wavelengths, discovering only 660 and 810 nm to have any effectiveness, whereas 732 and 980 nm did not. The third looked at varying regimens of daily laser treatments (1, 3, and 14 days) and found that 14 laser applications was excessive. We also review several studies of the effects of tLLLT on neuroprogenitor cells, brain-derived neurotrophic factor and synaptogenesis, immediate early response knockout mice, and tLLLT in combination therapy with metabolic inhibitors. CONCLUSIONS: Finally, some clinical studies in TBI patients are covered. FIG. 2. Functional mechanisms of transcranial LLLT. The gene transcription process described in can lead to decreases in neuronal apoptosis and excitotoxicity, and lessening of inflammation and edema, which will help reduce progressive brain damage. Increases in angiogenesis and expression of neurotrophins leading to activation of neural progenitor cells, and increased synaptogenesis may all contribute to the brain repairing itself from damage sustained in the trauma. Transcranial Low-Level Laser (Light) Therapy for Brain Injury Photomed Laser Surg. 2016 Dec 1;34(12):587-598. There are many such studies that show the efficacy of tLLLT in humans as well. It is virtually unknown in traditional neurological practice, but over the last year or two amazing results have been reported from around the globe. tLLLT has strong evidence for many beneficial effects on TBI and stroke in both animal models and human patients. Both acute stroke and acute TBI have a growing number of studies being published showing that tLLLT is an effective means of treating both. The many benefits of tLLLT are thought to be based on several different biological mechanisms: • Near-infrared PBM functions by improving mitochondrial energy production by stimulating the enzyme CCO and increasing ATP synthesis. • Laser therapy can result in neuroprotection and help prevent the spread of brain cell death after injury as shown by the long-term development of smaller lesion areas in mice treated with LLLT, when delivered at 4 h post-TBI. • Protection against toxins, increased cellular proliferation, and reduction in apoptosis and anti-inflammatory and antiedema effects may also contribute to the mechanisms that underlie the beneficial effects of PBM. • The most exciting prospect is the possibility that tLLLT may stimulate both neurogenesis (the ability of the brain to repair itself) and synaptogenesis (encourage cells to form new synaptic connections). This could lead to the application of tLLLT as a treatment modality for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. In South Africa up and coming neurologist Dr. Asheligh Bhanjan of Life Entabeni Hospital, Durban has a laser clinic for brain injured people. He reports astounding success with the therapy where severely brain injured individuals and stroke patients show remarkable recovery from their injuries. He also reports astonishing recoveries of people with Parkinson’s and Alsheimer’s. He also reports disappearance of pain for people living with constant pain. He is willing to be interviewed as has literally dozens of case studies and their families that are willing to speak. He has been a specialist for about 10 years, and admits that during his specializations years in Neurology they were not introduced to low-level light therapy for TBI or other conditions.
